answer.rationale: The binding constraints are: 14 days to contract expiry with no auto-renew, 94% line load with zero buffer, and an 18% spend mandate. That combination rules out switch_primary_vendor as the single decision this cycle even though memory_c2 records the largest cost win — a primary migration at zero buffer converts a cost problem into a delivery-stoppage problem, and c2's 'quick onboarding' was recorded under unknown load conditions. defer_decision (memory_c5) is inapplicable: c5 explicitly covers a NON-critical renewal that continued month-to-month; this contract does not auto-renew and the component is critical, so the analogy breaks. add_second_source (memory_c3) addresses concentration risk but does not deliver the 18% and leaves the expiring primary unresolved. That leaves negotiate_terms, but not as a price reopen — the incumbent has already refused that, so memory_c4's benchmarking play is largely spent this cycle. The live lever is memory_c6: term-for-price. A volume/duration commitment is a new deal structure rather than a reopen of this cycle's price, and c6 records it cutting unit cost without narrowing service scope and without migration work. I verify c6 to confirm the actual discount magnitude and whether it plausibly reaches 18% or only part of it, and c2 to check whether the low-cost vendor is qualified on this specific component and at what lead time — because that determines whether a switch is a viable next-cycle path or a dead end. Scale is deliberately guarded: a staged commitment with a short first tranche rather than a full multi-year lock, so we do not trade a one-year cost mandate for multi-year captivity to a supplier that has just demonstrated it will not move on price. Risks I am explicitly carrying forward: (1) every inherited memory is a recorded success, so this archive is survivorship-biased and silent on how these plays fail; (2) if the incumbent also refuses term-for-price, we reach expiry with no contract and no buffer, so a bridge extension must be secured in parallel as a floor, not left to the next review; (3) accepting a multi-year commit to hit a single-year finance target can raise true TCO and forecloses the second-source resilience that c3 says actually mattered during the shortage. I do not treat c6's outcome as guaranteed to repeat under a refusing incumbent.
